CG-025.reason: Vulnerability risk is ranked per finding of active, authorized assessments by a transparent additive score (0-100) rather than CVSS alone: exploitation evidence (CISA KEV 35; otherwise EPSS bands 28/20/10/3), exposure (network vector without user interaction on a reachable asset 25 internet / 18 network; needs user interaction 8; adjacent 10; local or physical 3; unknown 10), asset importance from asset.context (service criticality 15/11/6/2 plus restricted 5 or confidential 3 data; default 8 when no context) and CVSS severity (CVSS x 1.5, default 7). Existing controls subtract only when recorded with evidence: enforced network segmentation and blocked internet access (only for reachable findings), enforced entry MFA, operational monitoring (asset.compensating_controls) and an active EDR or antivirus with signatures at most 7 days old (agent.inventory_report), at most 20 points. Each finding lists every factor with its points and evidence in English and Arabic, marks missing inputs, flags KEV findings past the CISA due date, and shows its CVSS-only rank next to its risk rank; bands are critical >= 75, high >= 55, medium >= 35. Critical findings raise CG-VULN-RISK-025. The model is returned with every response and shown in the interface.

Low-impact authorized validation: only allow-listed read-only or single-request checks (version banner, credentialed config, credentialed patch, TLS configuration, safe port reachability, registry policy) and, when approved, an authorization reference, an approver, a window of at most 14 days, a rate limit of at most 60 per minute and at least one stop condition. Adversary emulation: only MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, only in a lab environment, and when approved two different approvers, isolation evidence and a rollback plan, within at most 30 days. Plans breaking a rule are rejected with a specific reason. Every validation.test_run is compared with its approved plan: unknown or unapproved plans, runs outside the window, techniques not in the plan and targets outside the plan (asset references or CIDR) are flagged out-of-plan, excluded from the plan results and alerted as CG-VALIDATION-OUT-OF-PLAN-026. scripts/Invoke-LowImpactValidation.ps1 performs a real low-impact validation of the local Windows host (SMBv1, RDP NLA, LLMNR, UAC, firewall profiles, antivirus signature age) using only registry reads and local cmdlets and writes a validation.test_run; CI runs it on the Windows runner. CyberGuard governs and records tests; it does not execute attacks.

CG-058.reason: Detection and response quality is measured, not asserted. Analysts and administrators record a disposition on each alert (true positive, benign true positive or false positive, with an optional note); the disposition resolves the alert, is audited and is kept per rule. /api/quality-metrics reports over a 1-365 day window: precision and false-positive rate overall and per rule (untriaged alerts are excluded and counted separately), MTTD from the earliest observed time of the evidence to the alert, MTTA, MTTR from the alert to its true or benign true positive disposition, and mean triage time (means and medians with sample counts); device coverage (assets on receiving sources and assets with evidence in the window, by source health); rule coverage (catalog rules whose evidence kind was received, rules fired, rules measured, noisy rules below 50% precision and blind rules with no evidence of their kind); and response failures (failed actions over completed actions, failures by action type, connector job failure rate and completion time per connector). Any metric without samples is reported as not measured instead of a number. The threats page shows these figures and the alert details offer the disposition.

CG-060.reason: CyberGuard keeps working through outages and reconciles afterwards instead of replaying blindly. It runs entirely locally (no internet dependency). Remote collectors deliver through scripts/forwarder.js (lib/forwarder.js): a durable on-disk queue with atomic enqueue and a size and depth limit, delivery in order, exponential backoff with jitter on network errors, 408, 429 and 5xx, and content refusals set aside in rejected/ with the reason instead of being retried forever or dropped; the source token comes only from CG_SOURCE_TOKEN. Delivery is idempotent: each (source, event_id) is stored once with its content hash, so a batch resent after a lost response is counted as duplicates, never stored twice, and a changed event under the same id is refused. Senders report queue depth and the oldest queued time with each batch; a backlog over one hour raises CG-DELIVERY-BACKLOG-060. Execute jobs not fetched by their connector within 60 minutes expire (CG-RESPONSE-STALE-060, audited) and need a new request and approval against current state, and a late result for them is refused; rollback jobs never expire, and a rollback counts only when the connector reports the restored state with evidence (post-rollback verification). /api/reconciliation and the response page list jobs awaiting connectors, expired jobs, failed and verified rollbacks and per-source delivery backlog; quality metrics count expiries separately from failures.

CG-065.reason: Published evidence is turned into detection hypotheses that are tested manually before approval; web text is never executed. lib/hypotheses.js accepts a hypothesis only as declarative data: a cited source (an HTTPS advisory or threat report, a known incident study from CG-064, or an internal observation), ATT&CK technique IDs, a severity, a rationale and up to ten conditions over one evidence kind using plain comparison operators (equals, not-equals, contains, starts-with, ends-with, in, gte, lte, exists) on validated field paths; any other field, operator, script or code-like field is refused. A new hypothesis is a draft that never alerts. The manual test requires labelled samples with at least one that must match and one that must not, a tester attestation of manual review, and replays the hypothesis over 30 days of stored evidence of its kind to show how often it would have fired; a failing test keeps it a draft. Only an administrator with recent MFA who is neither the author nor the tester can approve it; approved hypotheses are evaluated on new evidence and raise alerts under their own rule ID (CG-HYP-nnnn) linked to the evidence; retiring stops them. Every step is audited and the threats page manages the full workflow.

restrictions: Hypotheses evaluate one evidence kind per event; sequences across events remain built-in correlation rules. Signing and versioned rollback of approved rule changes are CG-066.

CG-066.reason: Detection rules and threat knowledge are updated under review, signing, kept versions and rollback. Each installation generates its own Ed25519 rule-signing key at runtime, stored owner-only in the data directory (lib/rule-signing.js). Every approved hypothesis version (CG-065) is stored as a signed canonical record with its approver; the running version is read from that record and its signature is verified before evaluation, so a version changed outside CyberGuard is not evaluated and raises CG-RULE-TAMPER-066 (critical). Changing an approved rule creates a new draft version that must pass its own manual test and independent approval while the approved version keeps running unchanged; alerts carry the version that raised them. An administrator with recent MFA can roll back immediately to any earlier signed version with a reason, audited. Threat knowledge moves between installations as a signed rule pack: export signs the running versions; import requires the publisher key to have been trusted by an administrator with recent MFA, refuses forged or altered packs, and creates every item as a draft that runs only after the local manual test and approval. The threats page shows running and latest versions with signature state, rollback buttons, trusted keys and pack import and export.

CG-067.reason: Every alert has a deterministic best-fix recommendation for its network environment and asset type, with limitations and uncertainty shown. lib/remediation.js maps the alert rule to an issue family (vulnerability, exposure, endpoint, identity, network, cloud, visibility, or a generic review for hypotheses and others) and lists the options in order (fix the root cause, upgrade or replace, mitigate, compensating control, contain with a typed response action) in Arabic and English. Options are adjusted to the recorded asset facts: network devices get management-plane and configuration-backup guidance, servers staging tests, endpoints managed deployment; ended vendor support makes patching not applicable with the reason and recommends upgrade or replacement; a critical service makes host isolation not applicable (contain at the network edge) and requires the recorded maintenance window or an agreed one; legacy compatibility profiles favour network controls; an active lab or pilot stage limits response scope. Each recommendation states how the fix will be verified, lists every unknown fact (asset type, operating system, vendor support, criticality, owner, evidence age) and sets the confidence from them, and states that it changes nothing. /api/alerts/:id/remediation serves it and the alert details window shows it.

CG-072.reason: External attack surface management covers registered and authorized assets only. scripts/attack-surface.js (lib/easm.js) runs on Linux, Windows and macOS from a scope file that must carry an authorization reference, an owner, an unexpired authorization window, address ranges no wider than /22 (IPv4) or /112 (IPv6), and domains whose ownership is proven by a DNS TXT token (cyberguard-verify=, generated by the token command) or declared with an ownership reference. It checks DNS A/AAAA/MX/TXT/CAA and SPF/DMARC, TLS certificates on TLS ports (expiry, self-signed, name coverage, legacy protocol, issuer, key type, fingerprint), reachable TCP services at a bounded rate, administrative and database services (SSH, Telnet, SMB, RDP, WinRM, VNC, database ports) and HTTP security headers (HSTS). Only addresses inside the authorized ranges are ever contacted: a domain that resolves elsewhere, or whose ownership is not verified, is recorded as not probed. With --nmap on Linux it uses nmap service detection on in-scope addresses only, at the scope rate; this runs for real in CI on Ubuntu. Nothing is exploited and no credentials are tried. Results become easm.observation evidence; each finding raises CG-EASM-072 with Arabic and English text and exposure remediation (CG-067); /api/attack-surface and the vulnerabilities page show targets, ownership, services, certificates, findings and not-probed addresses. A local self-check on the owner workstation found SMB, RDP and WinRM listening.

CG-074.reason: Preventive prioritization is based on asset importance, active exploitation (CISA KEV and EPSS), exposure and evidenced compensating controls (the CG-025 transparent risk model) and is now governed and measured rather than a CVE list. Every prioritized finding is tracked with its first-seen time, owner from the asset context and a remediation due date by risk band (critical 7, high 30, medium 90, low 180 days) or the earlier CISA KEV due date; escalation shortens the due date and a finding counts as fixed only when it disappears while an active assessment still covers the asset, so a closed assessment window is never reported as remediation. Overdue critical or high findings raise CG-VULN-SLA-074. Exceptions are time-boxed by band (30, 90 or 180 days), need a reason and the compensating control in place, are approved by an administrator with recent MFA, are audited and suspend the overdue state only until they expire. Quality is measured: open and overdue by band, exceptions, SLA compliance of resolved findings, mean days to remediate by band, median backlog age, findings fixed and risk reduced in 30 days, and the completeness of the prioritization inputs (exploitation intelligence, asset context, exposure evidence, owner). /api/vulnerability-governance and the vulnerabilities page show it with the exception workflow.

CG-092.reason: Suspicious files are examined without ever being executed (lib/file-triage.js, scripts/file-triage.js on Linux, Windows and macOS). For each file named on the command line it records SHA-256, SHA-1, MD5, size and file type from magic bytes; matches YARA rules with the installed yara tool (--yara, exercised for real on Ubuntu CI against the standard EICAR test file) or with a built-in subset available everywhere (text and hex strings, nocase, any/all/N of them) that refuses syntax it cannot evaluate instead of silently passing; verifies the publisher signature through Windows Authenticode (a real Microsoft-signed notepad.exe validates) and reports it as not available on other systems; and checks hash reputation against approved local known-bad and known-good lists with no internet lookup. The verdict is malicious, suspicious, trusted or unknown. With --quarantine and a reason, malicious files are moved byte-for-byte under their SHA-256 name, made read-only, re-hashed after the move and recorded in a hash-chained custody log with actor, host, time, original name, reason and case; verify-custody detects edits to the log or to a quarantined file. Results become file.triage evidence, raise CG-FILE-MALICIOUS-092 or CG-FILE-SUSPICIOUS-092 with endpoint remediation, and appear on the threats page.

CG-093.reason: Detonation and behavioural analysis happen only in a separate, isolated lab, under authorization controls, never against production and never automatically. CyberGuard executes no file; lib/sandbox.js governs jobs for an external sandbox (for example CAPE on a separate Linux host) that an administrator with recent MFA registers with an isolation reference and a dedicated sandbox-connector source, which cannot ingest telemetry. Detonation is disabled until such a sandbox exists. A job can be requested only by a person, only for a file quarantined by CG-092 (by SHA-256 and custody reference), and must be approved by a different administrator with recent MFA; no rule, hypothesis or AI path creates jobs. The sandbox fetches jobs with its own token only while its latest isolation self-check (no internet, no production reach, probe results, evidence reference) passed and is at most 24 hours old, and receives only the hash and custody reference, once. The behavioural report (processes, network attempts with blocked state, files, registry, signatures, verdict) must match the job hash; a malicious or suspicious verdict raises CG-SANDBOX-VERDICT-093, and any unblocked network attempt or failed self-check suspends the sandbox, cancels its approved jobs and raises critical CG-SANDBOX-ISOLATION-093. Every step is audited and the threats page shows sandboxes, isolation state and jobs with the approval buttons.

CG-094.reason: Linux security is covered through auditd, journald, eBPF and Falco where the kernel and support allow, plus sudo privilege and cron/systemd change monitoring. scripts/agent/linux-security.sh is a read-only collector (root gives the full view; unreadable items are reported, never guessed) that records auditd state and rule count, journald readability, eBPF support from the kernel version and BTF with the reason when it is limited or unavailable, the unprivileged BPF setting, Falco service state and driver unit, sudoers file fingerprints, NOPASSWD and full ALL grant counts, sudo/wheel/admin members, sudo use in the last 24 hours per user and command name from journald, and SHA-256 fingerprints of cron files and systemd service and timer units; file contents are never copied. CyberGuard validates this linux.security_posture evidence and compares each snapshot with the previous one for the host: added or modified cron/systemd persistence raises CG-LINUX-PERSIST-094, sudoers changes or NOPASSWD rules raise CG-LINUX-SUDO-094, and a host without a readable audit trail raises CG-LINUX-VISIBILITY-094. Falco JSON runtime alerts are a new log format (falco-json) mapped to IDS events with priority as severity. /api/linux-security and the sources page show coverage, sudo and changes. On Ubuntu CI the collector runs as root twice around a real cron file addition, and the change is detected and alerted.

CG-095.reason: macOS, iOS, Android and BYOD devices are covered through MDM, MAM and mobile EDR signals with each platform stating what it can and cannot see, and with user privacy protected. scripts/mdm-to-telemetry.js (lib/mdm.js) converts a read-only Microsoft Graph managedDevices export (Intune; other MDMs map to the same fields) into mdm.device_posture evidence: platform, OS version, ownership (corporate or personal), management type (MDM or MAM), compliance state, encryption, jailbreak or root signal, supervision, Mobile Threat Defense state and last check-in. Devices get a pseudonymous reference keyed by a private salt; personal devices keep no user name, device name, serial number, phone number, IMEI, location, apps or personal data, and CyberGuard refuses personal-device evidence that carries a name. Alerts: jailbroken or rooted device (high), noncompliant device, unencrypted corporate device and devices silent for over 7 days. /api/mobile-coverage and the sources page show counts per platform and a capability matrix per platform (for example iOS management cannot see other apps, processes, files or personal data; Android BYOD work profiles hide the personal profile), so a managed phone is never presented as fully monitored.

CG-096.reason: Network posture covers IPv4, IPv6, Wi-Fi, DNS/DHCP, VPN, VLAN, trunks, ACL, NAT and BGP/OSPF when needed and authorized, without assuming every configuration can be read. lib/network-posture.js and scripts/network-posture.js analyse an authorized, read-only running-config export (Cisco IOS / IOS-XE syntax) per area: IP source routing and proxy ARP; IPv6 enabled without traffic filters or RA guard; open or WEP SSIDs and WPA1 WLANs; a single DNS server or lookups without a server; DHCP snooping off while access ports exist; weak IKE (DES/3DES, MD5, DH groups 1/2/5) and ESP transform sets; active access ports in VLAN 1; DTP negotiation, trunks carrying all VLANs, native VLAN 1 and trunks still sending DTP; ACL entries permitting any IP; static NAT publishing inside services (administrative ports high); BGP neighbours without authentication or inbound route filters and OSPF without authentication. Each area reports assessed, not in configuration, not collected (sections the operator did not export) or not readable (authorization errors in the export); CyberGuard refuses findings for an area that was not assessed. Findings carry Arabic and English text, raise CG-NETPOSTURE-096 with remediation, and the network map shows per-area estate coverage and per-device detail.

CG-097.reason: Firewall review detects open any/any rules and shadowed and overlapping rules, distinguishes ingress, egress and east-west, and shows the impact before a modification. On top of the CG-020 analyser (duplicates, redundant and shadowed rules for first-match vendors, allows overridden by covering blocks for deny-overrides, any-any allows, broad inbound and administrative exposure, stale rules, expired exceptions), lib/firewall-analyzer.js now classifies every rule as ingress, egress or east-west from private and public address ranges and direction, reports per-device counts, and adds partial overlaps between rules with different actions (stating which rule wins the overlapping traffic), east-west rules that let any internal network reach any internal network on any port, east-west access to administrative ports, and unfiltered egress, each with Arabic detail. evaluate() decides a flow with the device semantics (first-match or deny-overrides, default deny), and whatIf() applies a proposed add, remove, disable, modify or move in memory against the latest stored ruleset and reports flows that would open or close, new and resolved findings and whether exposure increases, without changing anything. POST /api/firewall-rules/what-if validates the proposed rule strictly and returns the simulation; the policies page shows traffic classes per device and the impact form.

CG-098.reason: Zero Trust segmentation and NAC posture verify device and user authenticity and require a clear policy for new, guest and unmanaged devices. Each site declares a nac.policy (user authentication EAP-TLS, PEAP-MSCHAPv2, EAP-TTLS or none; device authentication certificate, MAB or none; unknown devices blocked, quarantined, guest or allowed; guest network isolation, sponsor and time limit; unmanaged devices denied, restricted or allowed; posture check; re-authentication interval; segment-to-segment reachability; evidence reference and review date), strictly validated. lib/nac-policy.js scores it out of 100 and reports missing device or user authentication, spoofable MAB-only device identity, PEAP-MSCHAPv2 credential capture risk, unknown or unmanaged devices with normal access, guests on the internal network, unbounded guest access, no posture check, infrequent re-authentication, segments that can reach every segment and stale reviews, in Arabic and English. The policy is compared with NAC authentications actually observed in FreeRADIUS logs over 30 days (802.1X successes, MAC-based logins, rejections, distinct devices): no observed authentications means enforcement is not confirmed, and MAC-based logins under a certificate policy are reported as drift. High gaps raise CG-NAC-POLICY-098; the network map lists sites by score and sites without a policy.

CG-099.reason: Network threat correlation combines DNS, TLS metadata, HTTP proxy, flow logs and network IDS, explaining the limits of encryption and monitoring and respecting privacy. Two new log formats are normalized: Zeek ssl.log (server name, TLS version, establishment, endpoints; no payload) and the Squid native access log, from which only the host is kept (paths and query strings are dropped). lib/network-correlation.js groups records per internal host and uses four anchors (IDS alert, algorithm-like domain by label length, digits and entropy, proxy block, TLS without a server name to an external address); a finding is raised only when at least one other independent source confirms the anchor within 15 minutes through the same domain or destination (for a DNS anchor the resolver is not taken as the destination), with confidence high from three sources. Each finding lists the internal host, anchor, destination, confirming sources, flow bytes and time span; non-low findings raise CG-NETCORR-099 once per correlation. The threats page shows which sources are present and the limits: payloads are not decrypted or stored, TLS 1.3 with Encrypted Client Hello hides the server name, QUIC and DNS over HTTPS or TLS bypass classic logs, proxy URLs are reduced to hosts, and flow logs show who talked to whom, not what was said.

CG-100.reason: OT/ICS safety mode reads passively first, blocks active scanning and default control of PLC, SCADA, BMS and other critical devices, has a separate safety approval interface and follows NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3. OT devices are registered as ot.asset_profile evidence (class PLC, RTU, SCADA/HMI, historian, engineering workstation, BMS, safety system, medical or other; Purdue level; industrial protocols; process impact; reachability from IT; remote access path; passive monitoring; controller logic backup) and assessed for IT reachability of control levels, direct remote access, missing passive monitoring, missing offline logic backups and unauthenticated control protocols reachable from IT (CG-OT-SAFETY-100 for the high ones). lib/ot-safety.js enforces: approved active validation plans (any tier other than passive) targeting OT assets or their addresses in production are refused; OT addresses are published as scan exclusions and the attack surface tool never contacts them (--ot-exclusions, not probed with reason ot-safety-exclusion); disruptive response actions on safety systems are refused at preview; and no response action on any OT asset is dispatched without a separate safety approval from an approver designated by an administrator with recent MFA, who is neither the requester nor the approver of the action, confirming the operator is on site, a manual fallback exists and the process is in a safe state or maintenance window; every decision is audited. The discovery page shows OT devices, findings, exclusions, approvers, pending safety approvals and the NIST SP 800-82 guidance in Arabic and English.

CG-101.reason: Before any network isolation the physical and network relationship IP -> MAC -> switch port -> VLAN -> user -> asset is verified, and trunk and uplink ports and shared virtualization hosts are avoided. scripts/port-map.js (lib/port-map.js) parses the text Cisco IOS / IOS-XE switches print for show ip arp, show mac address-table, show interfaces switchport and show lldp neighbors detail into network.port_map evidence. verifyPath() proves each link: the IP maps to exactly one MAC (several MACs are blocking as possible spoofing), the MAC is learned on exactly one access port (only on trunks or uplinks, or on several access ports, is blocking), the port is not an uplink to a switch, router or access point and does not serve a virtualization host (LLDP system description such as VMware ESX, Hyper-V, Proxmox) or more than two devices (an access port with one extra device is accepted as an IP phone), the learned VLAN matches the access or voice VLAN, the last NAC login on that MAC names the user, and the IP belongs to the asset. Shutting a switch port is accepted only when that exact port on that switch is a verified edge access port, and NAC quarantine only when the endpoint path verifies; the CG-029 response test now supplies port evidence. /api/assets/:id/network-path and the asset details window show each step as verified, unverified or blocking with Arabic text.

CG-102.reason: Management plane protection monitors and restricts SSH, RDP, WinRM, SNMP and VPN administration, enforces secure protocols and alerts on administrative access outside the approved procedure. A management.policy (lib/management-plane.js) names the covered devices by asset reference or network, the approved administrative sources (jump hosts or management networks), the approved protocols (SSH, RDP, WinRM, VPN, SNMPv3, HTTPS only; Telnet and SNMPv1/v2c cannot be approved), whether every session needs a change or ticket reference, and administrative hours. Every authenticated remote administration session (remote.authenticated evidence from CG-016 sources) on a covered device is checked as it arrives: an unknown or unapproved source, an unapproved protocol, a missing reference, or access outside the hours without an emergency reference raises CG-MGMT-ACCESS-102 with identity remediation. /api/management-plane and the network map list the last 7 days of sessions with their violations or as within the approved procedure or not covered, the devices whose configurations still enable insecure management protocols (Telnet, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c from the CG-021 checks) and secure-protocol guidance in Arabic and English.

CG-103.reason: An OCSF normalization layer converts multi-vendor events into OCSF 1.3.0 while tracking schema version, event source, missing fields and meaning lost in conversion. lib/ocsf.js maps every normalized log record to an OCSF class (Authentication 3002 for NAC, ZTNA and VPN; Network Activity 4001 for flows, firewall and TLS metadata; HTTP Activity 4002 for proxy; DNS Activity 4003; DHCP Activity 4004; Detection Finding 2004 for IDS and WAF; API Activity 6003 for cloud audit; Base Event 0 for generic syslog) with category, activity, type_uid, severity_id, status, endpoints, user, query, TLS, traffic, HTTP request and response, finding info and disposition, and metadata carrying the OCSF version, the original format, the product and log name and the original time. Each record states the fields its class needs that the source lacked and the meaning lost (severity scales mapped, proxy URL paths and query strings dropped for privacy, TLS certificate details absent, no specific class for generic syslog). GET /api/ocsf/export returns the events for a 1-720 hour window and per format and class quality (records, missing fields, lossy records, complete or incomplete); the events page shows the quality table and the download link. The Squid parser now keeps the HTTP method so the OCSF activity is correct.

CG-121.reason: Prompt-injection defense. lib/prompt-guard.js treats logs, mail, tickets, search results and all evidence as untrusted data. Text reaches a model only through envelope(): the fixed system policy (with its SHA-256) is separate, and each item is a labelled untrusted DATA block with its source, hash and findings, cleaned of hidden characters and role markers, closed by a per-request random boundary that the data cannot forge. The AI analysis now reports evidence that carries instructions, raises CG-AI-INJECTION-121 (mapped to MITRE ATLAS AML.T0051) and withholds suggestions whose target appears only in instructing evidence; model-connector proposals are refused when their rationale carries instructions or their target is tainted, and cloud model answers that carry instructions or commands are refused (CG-039 typed-only gateway still applies). Every refusal is audited. /api/ai-guard shows the policy hash, patterns, flagged evidence and refusals; /api/ai-guard/scan lets connectors submit text and get it back as cleaned untrusted data with findings. The AI analyst page shows the defense and a scan form.

CG-122.reason: Evidence-grounded AI answers. lib/evidence-rag.js grounds every /api/ai-analysis answer: each cited source (stored event, matched rule, alert, asset, advisory, playbook) is captured as a dated snapshot with a SHA-256, reused when the source is unchanged, and the answer is stored append-only with its own hash, so it can be reopened later (/api/ai-answers/:id) with its answer and every snapshot verified intact. What a reader sees is redacted for their role: secrets (AWS keys, tokens, bearer and JWT values, private keys, password assignments) are hidden for everyone; viewers do not see accounts, email, phone, national identity numbers or internal addresses; analysts see accounts and addresses with email partly masked and phone and identity numbers hidden; admins see phone and identity numbers partly masked. CG-131.reason: Network change safety and Batfish research. lib/change-safety.js keeps a register of required flows (source, destination, protocol and port, devices on the path, criticality) and, before an ACL, firewall or route change, evaluates every flow against the latest stored snapshot of each device on its path (firewall ruleset and discovered routes) and against the snapshot with the proposed change applied: the flow breaks (allowed before, denied or without a route after), opens, changes path (another next hop by longest-prefix match) or cannot be verified. CG-171.reason: Blast radius calculator. lib/blast-radius.js gives a specific warning before four changes, from visible relationships only: stopping a service (infrastructure roles from the CG-133 impact graph, business service and owner, distinct clients in flow logs over seven days), shutting a switch port (devices learned on the port, LLDP neighbour and their roles), disabling a user (sign-ins, remote sessions and their hosts, applications and SaaS services running as the account, permissions used over 30 days) and changing a cloud security group (resources that reference it in the cloud inventory, which now accepts security_groups per resource, public exposure and business services). Each result states what it is based on and its level (none, limited, broad); when no relationship is visible the impact is unknown and requires human review, so missing data is never reported as no impact. POST /api/blast-radius and the response page form show it in Arabic and English.
tests: tests/blast-radius.test.js: stop service, switch port, disable user and security group changes get a specific blast radius from visible relationships, and unknown when none is visible (CG-171)
tests/ui-contract.test.js: the response page offers the blast radius calculator for the four change types with unknown needing human review (CG-171)
restrictions: The calculator assesses; disabling users and changing security groups are not response actions in CyberGuard. The level thresholds (up to five affected items is limited) are a heuristic shown with the items themselves.

CG-172.reason: Just-in-time rule lease engine. lib/rule-lease.js keeps leases with an explicit scope (asset, source, destination, protocol, port; wildcards refused), TTL, owner, change ticket, a different approving administrator with recent MFA and a revocation deadline (expiry plus 15 minutes). Expiry is enforced on the enforcement layer: the installing response connector reports response.lease_state with the device-side expiry timer, and a lease is installed only when that timer is at or before the approved expiry; otherwise it is flagged with a high alert. Reconciliation runs on every device report and on every health check, so after a CyberGuard outage leases past their revocation deadline without confirmed removal become overdue (high alert), rules the device holds with no lease are orphans, and rules removed before expiry are shown as removed early; a later removal report closes an overdue lease as expired on the device. CG-LEASE-172 covers these alerts and the response page shows leases in Arabic and English.
tests: tests/rule-lease.test.js: leases are exact, ticketed and second-approved, expire on the enforcement layer, and reconciliation finds overdue, unenforced, orphan and early-removed rules after an outage (CG-172)
tests/ui-contract.test.js: the response page shows rule leases with approved expiry, device timer, revocation deadline and reconciled status (CG-172)

CG-173.reason: Evidence-backed action ledger. lib/action-ledger.js builds one entry per response command joining who requested, approved, safety-approved, dispatched and (as a named connector) executed it; why (reason, trigger as AI proposal on an alert or manual request, the alert); the ticket (authorization reference); the evidence events of the alert with their hashes; the preflight (dry-run hash, before state, recovery plan hash); the API result (connector, request hash, status, phase, completion); the independent outcome verification (CG-118); the rollback steps; and the action timeline with audit hashes. Every string passes the secret redactor and an extra password, pin and passphrase scan, so no password reaches the ledger. Entries are SHA-256 chained in request order and verifyLedger detects a changed entry at its position. GET /api/action-ledger, an export, and the response page show it in Arabic and English.
tests: tests/action-ledger.test.js: every command is one hash-chained ledger entry with who, why, ticket, evidence, preflight, API result, outcome and rollback, and no password reaches it (CG-173)
tests/ui-contract.test.js: the response page shows the evidence-backed action ledger with chain head and export (CG-173)
restrictions: The ledger is derived from the stored records on request; its chain protects the export, while the underlying audit log keeps its own hash chain.

CG-174.reason: No single-action critical shutdown. lib/critical-shutdown.js identifies critical assets (domain controller, core switch or uplink, backup controller, ESXi/Hyper-V host, security platform) from owner declarations, the domain-controller device type and impact-graph roles. A disruptive action (isolate, shut down, stop/disable/remove service, port shutdown, NAC quarantine, cloud isolation) on a critical asset is refused unless it is the next step of an approved composite plan: 2 to 10 ordered steps, a change reference, and either a maintenance window or out-of-band recovery with owner and evidence, approved by two administrators other than the requester with recent MFA. Steps are used once and in order, only inside the window and before expiry, and a completed plan cannot be replayed. The existing protected-role refusal for domain controllers stays unless an approved plan covers the step. The response page shows critical assets and plans in Arabic and English. This release also makes the CG-173 ledger test deterministic: its redaction check used a value that could appear by chance in random hex identifiers.

tests/ui-contract.test.js: the response page shows critical assets and composite plans with two approvals and window or out-of-band recovery (CG-174)
restrictions: Plans govern CyberGuard response actions only; changes made outside CyberGuard are not covered. Out-of-band recovery is recorded as declared evidence, not tested by CyberGuard.
